title: Bigger barns (Luke 12:13–21)
hook: a rich man plans his retirement and dies that night

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman blessed his mother, and he blessed everyone who keeps the word. Your line was hear and keep it.

It starts with a family fight. Someone in the crowd shouts at Jesus: Master, tell my brother to split the inheritance with me. It's the tone of siblings across a lawyer's table after a funeral. Jesus won't be the judge. Who made me a divider over you? He turns to the crowd: beware of all covetousness, because a man's life does not consist in the abundance of things he possesses. Then he tells a story about a farmer whose year went very, very well.
screen: `TELL MY BROTHER TO SPLIT IT.` → `WHO MADE ME A DIVIDER?` → `A FARMER'S VERY GOOD YEAR.`

segments.voice: A rich man's land brings in a huge harvest, and he has nowhere to put it all. So he talks to himself, and Luke lets us listen. What shall I do? I know. I will pull down my barns and build greater, and store everything there. And I'll say to my soul: soul, you have plenty laid up for many years, take your rest, eat, drink, enjoy yourself. Notice who he's talking to. My crops, my barns, my goods, my soul. Nobody else is in the room: not his workers, not his neighbors, not the hungry, not God. Then God speaks into the room: "Thou fool, this night do they require thy soul of thee: and whose shall those things be which thou hast provided?" He planned a retirement and didn't get an evening. And the question cuts back to the brothers at the start: whose will it all be? Jesus finishes: so is he that lays up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God. He isn't a fool for having a good harvest or for planning ahead. Joseph stored grain in Egypt and saved lives. He's a fool because the harvest only ever went into barns. Saint Basil the Great, preaching on this parable, put it bluntly: the extra bread you store belongs to the hungry, and the shoes rotting in your closet belong to someone barefoot. The Catechism calls this the universal destination of goods: what we own is meant, in the end, to serve everyone.
screen: `A HARVEST WITH NOWHERE TO GO.` · `MY CROPS, MY BARNS, MY SOUL.` · `RICH TOWARD GOD.` · `BASIL: THE EXTRA BREAD IS THEIRS.` · then, large: `THOU FOOL, THIS NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Picture your own barns: a garage, a shelf, a savings account, a pile kept for someday, and walk through them slowly in your mind. Notice one thing you aren't using that somebody else could: a set of tools, a sum of money, an hour you could give. If you pray, ask to be rich toward God.
Bigger barns. The rich farmer's plan to store everything for himself, and God's answer: this night your soul is required of you. Today's word.
Your line: this night. Not many years from now, but this very evening. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the rich fool at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel, and Catholic social teaching speaks of the universal destination of goods: private property is real, but its use is meant to serve the common good.

chat.says: Was the rich farmer a fool just for saving up his harvest?
options: No, planning was fine; it all went into his barns, never toward God or others.
Yes, Jesus taught that saving anything for the future is a sin.
No, his only mistake was building the new barns far too slowly.
